title.en: Granny Jinny: the Bee-King and the Aunties
title.zh: 賈妮奶奶：蜂王與眾姨婆

region.en: Southwest Missouri Ozark country, USA (symbolic pin: Joplin area)
region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶（象徵定位：喬普林一帶）

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales, as Told Among the Negroes of the South-West' (1893), chapter I 'The Bee-King and the Aunties' (told by 'Granny', Aunt Mary, Big Angie and the circle at the cabin fire)

summary.en: A convention of witches that is only Granny's company: a hundred-year-old woman born at Culpepper Court-house in Ole Feginny who has seen General Washington, claims descent from the Lenni-Lenape, and holds every power the quarter reveres — setting hens, out-generalizing turkeys, telling crops by the moon, laying out the dead, interpreting dreams, seeing ghosts and withstanding devils, patting Juba and jumping Jim Crow — while around the hickory-blaze sit Big Angie and the aunties, the surviving court of her authority.
summary.zh: 一場看似巫會的聚會，其實是賈妮奶奶的『待客會』：百歲高齡、生於老弗吉尼亞庫爾佩珀縣、親見過華盛頓將軍，自稱源出萊尼-勒納佩族；舉凡孵雞、馴野火雞、觀月令卜種、為亡者整容、解夢、見鬼抗魔、踏朱巴步、跳吉姆·克勞舞——鄉里敬畏的本領她樣樣在行；炭火四週坐著大安琪與眾姨婆，如同她權威的朝堂。

sensitivity.note: Frame-narrative portrait of the tale-telling circle from Owen's Missouri fieldwork (teller named as 'Granny', born in Virginia, claimed Indian descent); recorded as folkloric characterization, not as ritual instruction.

passages.text: It was not a convention of witches, though it bore the outward seeming of one; it was Aunt Jinny's 'company', and a good time the guests were having too. Aunt Jinny, or as her intimates called her, Granny, sat in the middle of the semicircle drawn round the great fireplace ablaze with the conflagration of a quarter of a cord of hickory logs, and felt herself as important a mistress of the situation, there in her cabin, as any queen could in her palace of carved stone. A great authority in her way was Granny.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, Voodoo Tales, chapter I (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: She knew the value of every herb and simple to be found in the state; she was an adept in the healing art; she could 'set' hens so that they never lost an egg; she could out-general the shyest turkey that ever stole its nest in the weeds and brush; she could tell when to wean a calf or baby and when to plant crops by the age and position of the moon; she could lay out the dead and usher in the living; she could interpret dreams; she knew the sign of everything from the spilling of salt to the flight of birds; she had seen ghosts and withstood devils; she knew legends and tales without number; and, last and most important, she was, to quote her own words, 'bornded at Culpepper Court-house in Ole Feginny and had seen Gin'al Washington with my own eyes' — and she was sold once and fetched a heap of money, and would again, being over a hundred years old and spry, for only shiftless critters that are cheap from the start wear out early.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter I, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her claims to aristocracy were always acknowledged by her associates: bond and now free, they agreed that all the past glories and dignities of her former owners up at The House were centred and kept alive in her own proper person; and her lineage was believed in without a demur — accepted as a child of the Werowances, though her abundant grey wool was of the woolliest, and ordinarily she appeared in a short cotton costume, a Madras turban very much awry, and a pair of men's boots much the worse for wear, carrying a stout hickory staff — 'I wears ole master's boots and hats; what's good 'nuff for him is good 'nuff for me.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter I, ending (1893); not verbatim.

region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter XII 'Luck-Balls' (Aunt Mymee's lost fetich; told in the cabin circle)

summary.en: The horror of losing a luck-ball — the yarn fetich talked to by its owner's own name, in which her soul as well as her luck lived: found by the child Tow Head in a dirty linen bag, restored against Mymee's naked skin under the arm, and fed its weekly drink of eau-de-vie from a black bottle, the string mended and slung over the left shoulder — while Granny and Aunt Mary, who had begun to enjoy the terror, have to laugh out of the other side of the mouth.
summary.zh: 丟失幸運球的恐怖——那個以主人名字相喚、藏著她靈魂與運氣的線團法物：被孩子『蓬頭』從髒布袋中尋回、貼著裸膚掛回腋下、每週喂一次黑瓶裡的『生命之水』，斷繩接好斜掛肩上——而正樂得看熱鬧的賈妮與瑪麗姨婆，只得笑不出聲了。

sensitivity.note: Hoodoo charm-material recorded at folklore level by Owen (Leland's note: the incident occurred to his own family's cook). No preparation instructions beyond what the source itself records as practice; presented here as documentary folk belief. The underlying practice is a living tradition; nothing beyond the source's public content is reproduced.

passages.text: Aunt Mymee had been in what Granny designated as a terrible taking — the cause being the loss of her most powerful fetich, the luck-ball she had talked to and called by her own name as if it were her double. Her superstitious terrors when she discovered the loss were really pitiable; her overbearing manner toward the other negroes quite forsook her, her limbs were palsied and her complexion bleached to that awful greyish pallor. She had missed the precious ball in the morning when she was dressing herself, hastily felt in her bed, snatched off the covers and shook the pillows vigorously, scrutinized the floor — no ball could be found. Then Aunt Mymee went wild: her morning duties were forgotten, she ran hither and thither looking in all possible and impossible places of concealment, obstinately refusing to state what she had lost; finally, with a groan of despair, she flung herself down on her cabin floor in a cowering heap and quavered out that she would be better off in her grave, for an enemy had stolen her luck-ball, and her soul as well as her luck was in it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Her daughter's pickaninnies spread the news in great excitement; but scarcely had Granny and Aunt Mary begun to enjoy it when they had to laugh out of the other side of the mouth — Tow Head proudly marched to the cabin with an exceedingly dirty little bag in her hand, desiring to know if Aunt Mymee's soul was tied up in that nasty thing. Evidently it was: Aunt Mymee sprang up with a joyful cry, kissed the bag and hugged the finder, then sternly demanded how she got it without her knowing — 'Found it by my bed this morning. I didn't show that ball under the sun; when I was telling her about Uncle John's Jack she told me never to say anything more about such wicked idol-ery, and I promised I wouldn't, and I always keep my promises — if I don't forget.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Aunt Mymee heaved a sigh of relief — 'That is a good child, don't pester your ma' — and began to fumble at the strings wrapped (not tied) round the neck of the dirty bag that had raised such a commotion. She was going to give Lil Mymee a drink: that ball does not sip water but sups what Big Angy calls eau-de-vie, and that surely is the water of life, for if she does not get it she dies. She produced the black bottle of Little Mymee's elixir — better known to the general public as whiskey — and proceeded to moisten first the ball, then herself; after which ceremony she restored the ball to its proper receptacle, mended the broken string that had been the cause of its loss, and made it an ornament to her person by slinging the string over her left shoulder and under her right so that the ball rested under her right armpit — having, beforehand, slipped out of the various waists of her raiment, so that the ball should lie against her naked body with no intervening fold of calico to absorb its strength.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: King A, the Voodoo Doctor Who Travels on the Devil's Steed
title.zh: A王：騎魔馬而行的伏都醫者

region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter XII 'Luck-Balls' (portrait of 'King' A, a Voodoo doctor or conjurer)

summary.en: The maker of the luck-balls is a curious half-barbarian who never stays long in a place, makes his entrances secretly and mysteriously in the night, never confides in anyone, never spends money for anything but whiskey, and never lacks for the good things of this world nor is reduced to begging or stealing — no cabin refuses him shelter and the best bed and food it can afford; no one knows whence he came or whither he is going. When four taps are heard above the latch, someone flies to usher in the guest: 'A is there' is the unspoken conviction, and it is generally conceded that he travels at his ease on some strange steed of the devil's providing.
summary.zh: 幸運球的製者是一位奇特的半野蠻人：從不長居一地、夜半神秘而來、從不吐露心事、錢只花在威士忌上，卻從不缺世間好物，也從不乞討偷竊——沒有一間小屋會拒絕給他最好的床與食；無人知其來處去向。閂上有四下輕叩，便有人飛身開門：『A王到了』是不言自明的信念；眾人皆信他騎著魔鬼所賜的怪馬自在行路。

sensitivity.note: Portrait of a named (initial) conjure-doctor from Owen's Missouri fieldwork; recorded as folkloric legend about a living figure of the 1890s, without reproducing any working ritual.

passages.text: How the luck-ball was made, and what were its components, Tow Head did not at that time know, though she gathered from the half-whispered gossip of the other aunties that it was the work of 'King' A, a Voodoo doctor or conjurer of great powers and influence. This A was a curious half-barbarian who never stayed long in a place, made his entrances secretly and mysteriously in the night, never confided in any one, never spent money for anything but whiskey, never lacked for the good things of this world, and never was reduced to the inconvenience of begging or stealing, although he was like the lilies of the field that toil not, neither do they spin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: No cabin refused him shelter and the best bed and food it could afford. No one knew whence he came or whither he was going. When four taps were heard above the latch, some one flew to usher in the guest; 'A is there' was the unspoken conviction. How he came was a matter of conjecture: it was generally conceded that he travelled at his ease on some strange steed of the devil's providing — and as soon as he was settled in his temporary quarters, that is, had eaten of everything in the larder and drunk generous potations, he was gone again into the night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XII, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Ole Blue Jay: the Sand-Carrier of Hell

region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter IX 'Some Tales in Which Blue Jay and His Gwines-On Figure Conspicuously' (told by Granny)

summary.en: Granny's cosmology of gossip: every Friday Ole Blue Jay goes to Hell with sand and the account of all the bad folks' doings; he builds up the walls of the Bad Place, gives out the news to the Ole Boy, loads himself with all the lies he can tote, and comes back among us — and when he turns the lies loose the Lord knows it makes no end of quarrelling and fussing. The mocking-bird, sick with only one tune, served thejay his come-uppance for his impertinence, and so learned to learn more tunes.
summary.zh: 賈妮奶奶的饞舌宇宙論：每逢禮拜五，老藍鶺便帶著沙土與眾惡人的劣跡簿下地獄；他築起『壞地方』的城牆，把消息呈給老魔頭，再負上滿載的謊言回到人間——謊言一放，吵鬧與口角便無窮無盡。嘲鶇先生因只有一支曲子鬱鬱而病，替老婆出氣教訓了無禮的藍鶺，也由此學會了更多的曲子。

sensitivity.note: Cosmological-burlesque bird tale from Granny's repertoire. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Granny had got a heap better tale than any rabbit tale, studied out in the night until it roused her so she did not get a wink of rest since the chickens crowed for midnight — a tale about Ole Blue Jay. 'And he is the one that goes to Hell of a Friday and carries sand and the account of all the bad folkses' do; and when he takes that sand and builds up the walls of the Bad Place and then gives out all the bad news to the Ole Boy, then he loads himself up with all the lies that he can tote and comes back among us. Much account, huh? — when he gets back and turns those lies loose, the Lord knows it makes no end of quarrelling and fussing!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter IX (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was along of Ole Blue Jay — him that thinks himself so smart and really was a plum fool — that the new tunes came to the mocking-bird. In the old good times, when possum grease and sweet-potatoes were as plenty as doodle-bugs and cockle-burs, the mocking-birds did not know but just one tune; and the reason they know more now is this. Mister Mocking-bird was sitting home with a misery in his back and a cold in his head and a squawmishness in his stomach, and could not sing even the one tune he knew; Miss Mocking-bird had to fly round and do the marketing her own self.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter IX, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the times she had been out abroad hunting up something that would lay on her ole man's stomach, she met up with Ole Blue Jay, who offered — mighty soft — to carry her vegetables home, for it would be a burning shame for a slim young person to tote a load that would make her lopsided and spoil that fine form of hers. At that she just laughed and flew off with the truck; and when she got home she told her ole man, and he flared up and said he was going to give Blue Jay a licking for his impudence — and then he sort of trimmed up his feathers and said he did not know but that he felt his strength coming back some. From that minute he began to mend, and went to the market next morning himself — and the mocking-bird never knew but one tune again, but one was never enough for him after that.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter IX, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Ole Rabbit and the Dog He Stole: Gopher's Winter Supplies
title.zh: 老兔與他偷的狗：鼠鼴的過冬存糧

region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter X 'Ole Rabbit an' de Dawg he Stole — How He Obtained Gopher's Winter Supplies' (told by Granny)

summary.en: Ole Rabbit, gorged on Gopher's cellar of sweet shoots and calamus, hears of Gopher's dainties — bumble-bee honey, Sunday vittles — and proposes an exchange of goods: he will show Gopher his truck-patch, a splendid pile he has 'sot out and worked' by his own overseering. The pile is dog-roots and wilted trash raked from the crumbling creek bank; while Gopher blinks sun-blind underground hauling the rubbige down, Rabbit unhurries the good roots into the brier-patch — and the family camps out there till the hounds and the scandal both cool.
summary.zh: 老兔吃遍鼠鼴窖中的嫩莖菖蒲，又聽說蜂蜜與安息日大菜，便提議以貨易貨：帶他去看自家的『作物堆』——其實是從河岸朽根與蔫草堆起的『豐收』。趁鼠鼴在地下被日頭晃得暈頭轉向地把垃圾往下運，老兔慢條斯理把好根藏進荊棘窩——一家老小在窩裡紮營，直到獵犬與閒話一併冷卻。

sensitivity.note: Rabbit-swindle tale from Granny's repertoire. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Hearing of Gopher's dainties — 'bummle-bee honey' and the rest, which Gopher offered sort of hanging back with the words as if most ashamed to let them out — nearly killed Ole Rabbit, but since he was filled up in the corners with those white shoots and calamus he could stand it better when the chat ran on vittles; so he looked mighty and tossed up his chin, cleared his throat, as if the naming of common vittles made him contemptuous, and said that if Gopher was not satisfied he might fetch in some of his truck when the day got more along toward noon and warmer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeming to Gopher like he would perish if he did not get some of that truck, he agreed mighty fierce-eagerly, and began throwing out the truck he had in the cellar; then him and Ole Rabbit made the agreement that when the cellar was all cleared out, Ole Rabbit would show him the way to the truck-patch. With that saying Ole Rabbit went out — but he did not go home, for what was the use, there was no pot a-boiling in his house that day: he was just telling outrageous lies to get Gopher all tore up in his mind, and he done it. Instead of going home he went down by the creek where the bank crumbles off and the water washes the roots of the weeds and briars out; he lopped off heaps of dog-roots and piled them up in a big pile out in a field, then got a very big lot of wilted-trash and piled them on too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then he loped back and asked Gopher to come along, since he was through his big dinner and had nothing a-libbing thing to do except to help a friendly man — which was certainly a pleasure instead of a bother. 'Here it is, neighbor! I done sot him out and worked him and laid him by my own-self, so I know just what you are getting.' Gopher, winking and blinking in the sun till he could not tell a tater from a toadstool, took Rabbit's word for it and got to work; while Gopher took the first load down cellar his own self, Rabbit — a-turning his back and stuffing his handkerchief in his mouth to keep from bursting out laughing — grabbed up an armful of those nice sweet roots and goobers and hid them in the brush nigh home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X, ending (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: They kept up that foolishness till sundown; then Rabbit loped off home and told the ole woman and the children they had better camp in the brier-patch that night and the next day, because the hounds were out — and they were more than willing when they heard that, and more than willing to say so when they caught sight of Gopher's truck in there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter X, ending (1893); not verbatim.

title.en: Ole Woodpecker and the Blind Bear-Mammy
title.zh: 老啄木鳥與瞎眼熊媽媽

region.zh: 美國密蘇里西南歐扎克地帶

source.work: Mary Alicia Owen, 'Voodoo Tales' (1893), chapter XIX 'The Last Gleaning of the Field' (the tale of the two bears and Ole Woodpecker, told by Aunt Em'ly)

summary.en: The widow-bear, blinded by a cold got fishing, is starved by her housemate the old maid bear, who keeps the good meat on the high swinging shelf in the cellar where poor old blind mammy cannot find it — until Ole Woodpecker, knocking round among the shingles, peeks down the chimney, calls himself a poor little boy stuck in the chimney, and when the groping mammy comes to help, flings a charm spang in her face that fetches back her sight quick enough to see Woodpecker clear out of the chimney.
summary.zh: 漁時受寒失明的寡婦熊，被同居的老處女熊剋扣口糧——好肉全鎖在窖中高懸架上，瞎眼的老媽媽永遠摸不著。老啄木鳥在瓦片間敲擊時自煙囪窺破一切，自稱『可憐的小男孩卡在煙囪裡』，哄得瞎媽媽摸索救助；趁機把一枚符物迎面擲去——視力立返，她親眼看著啄木鳥飛出煙囪逃之夭夭。

sensitivity.note: Animal-helper tale from Aunt Em'ly's repertoire. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: There was once an old mammy bear that was a widow-bear, and as she was going along through the woods one time — it was along in the spring-time — she met up with another bear that was an old maid. After they had asked one another howdy and passed the time of day, saying how they felt lonesome now their families were all broke up, they sort of agreed and made it up that they would keep house together during the warm weather. So say, so do, and they settled down together, and hunted and fished and divided evenly and fair — until the widow-bear took a cold from getting her feet wet fishing, and it settled in her eyes and by and by put them clean out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XIX (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: That was a bad time for Miss Bear. There she was in her own house, but the old maid bear fetched her nothing but the bones: all the good meat she did not eat right up she kept on the high swinging shelf in the cellar, where poor old blind mammy could not find it. Mammy sort of suspected something, but there she was, and no use to say nothing, but she got leaner and leaner all the time, till her bones rattled when the wind blew and her hide flopped like a flag on the hill-top. If it had not been for Ole Woodpecker, old mammy would have naturally given up the ghost — but he was a-knocking round among the shingles on the roof, and he heard the old mammy sniffing and crying (the old maid was out a-hunting), and he peeked down the chimney and saw just how it was.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XIX, middle (1893); not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Never mind! I fix that,' he said, and hollered down, 'Hello, mammy! come help me.' She stopped crying and asked who he was. 'I am a poor little boy got stuck in your chimney.' Instead of scolding like the old maid would have done, poor ole mammy groped to the chimney and felt round to help. 'Poor child,' she said, 'I am feared I cannot do much. Holler again so I can tell just where you is, because I am blind, honey.' He hollered and hollered and kept the old mammy feeling round till she was distracted; then, all of a sudden, he flung a charm spang in her face that fetched back her sight that quick, that she saw Ole Woodpecker fly out of that chimney and clear out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Owen, chapter XIX, ending (1893); not verbatim.
